newsitem.title: USA: Albright, EU stress importance of strong ties.
newsitem.headline: Albright, EU stress importance of strong ties.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and European Union officials on Tuesday stressed the importance of strong U.S.-EU ties and their determination to intensify trans-Atlantic cooperation.

After talks at the State Department, Albright's spokesman said the ministers agreed to keep pressure on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to honour elections won by the political opposition and to support the United Nations playing a key role in lowering tensions on Cyprus.

But there were no suggestions any decisions were taken on how to deal with China's human rights record when the U.N. Human Rights Commission meets in Geneva in March or on divisions remaining over a controversial U.S. anti-Cuba law.
The visit to Washington by Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo and European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan began an EU campaign to paper over cracks in the trans-Atlantic relationship.
The EU has said it is committed to improving ties with Washington after a year strained by trade disputes.

Albright, at a short news conference with Van Mierlo and Brittan, said U.S.-EU relations are vital "to the overall health and potency of the international system" and cooperation between them raises standards around the globe.
"Our talks focused on how we can further deepen our already successful cooperation on a wide range of foreign policy concerns," she said, without being specific.
Van Mierlo said during the Cold War, U.S.-European ties were "self-evident" but no more. Now, "we have to invest in the relation if we want to keep up the relation," he said.

One year has passed since the EU and the United States signed a new trans-Atlantic agenda and "it is now time to show that international cooperation is yielding results," with special focus on international crime, central and eastern Europe, the Middle East and the former Yugoslavia, he said.
Brittan said while progress has been on economic issues, it is time to focus on "some of the great issues of a political kind...particularly the question of China."
Van Mierlo said: "I don't see that much divergence on Bosnia" between the United States and Europe. As for NATO enlargement, "that is a fact of history," he said.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said "there was an agreement that the European countries and the United States need to keep Milosevic's feet to the fire," meaning pressure must be maintained on the Serbian leader to accept elections won by the political opposition.

There was also a long discussion about the "importance of Turkey's role in Europe" and the need for the United States and the EU to have a "common position" on whether a resolution criticising China's human rights record should be proposed at the U.N. commission meeting in Geneva, he said.
